Laughter
LAF-ter
n.
From laugh, Saxon hlihhan. Webster 1828: convulsive merriment; an expression of mirth peculiar to man. Scripture treats it as both a gift of God in deliverance and a mask over a sorrowful heart, and Ecclesiastes calls it mad.

Biblical Definition

Laughter in Scripture is neither condemned nor simply commended; it is weighed, and the weighing is unusually shrewd. At its best it is the involuntary response of a delivered people: When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The LORD hath done great things for them (Psalm 126:1-2). That laughter is a form of praise and the nations recognise it as such. But Proverbs observes what laughter often covers: Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness (Proverbs 14:13). The Preacher, who tested every pleasure deliberately, returns a hard verdict: I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it? (Ecclesiastes 2:2), and states the reason elsewhere — Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better (Ecclesiastes 7:3). James applies this pastorally to a worldly church: Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness (James 4:9), which is a call to repentance rather than to gloom.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LAUGHTER as convulsive merriment; an expression of mirth peculiar to the human species, consisting in a peculiar noise and motion of the muscles of the face and body; also, an expression of scorn or contempt.

expand to see more

LAUGHTER, n. — Convulsive merriment; an expression of mirth peculiar to man, attended by a peculiar noise and motion of the features.

The expression of joy or gladness; as, the mouth filled with laughter.

Sometimes an expression of scorn, derision, or contempt; as, to hold a thing in laughter.

Distinguished by moralists from cheerfulness, which is habitual, laughter being sudden and transient.

From Saxon hlehter, from hlihhan, to laugh — probably imitative in origin.

Key Scripture

Psalm 126:2 — "Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The LORD hath done great things for them."

Proverbs 14:13 — "Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness."

Ecclesiastes 2:2 — "I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?"

Ecclesiastes 7:3 — "Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better."

James 4:9 — "Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness."

Modern Corruption

A church shaped by entertainment has made continuous levity the mark of an approachable ministry, and James 4:9 addresses precisely such a congregation with a command that no modern service would dare to obey.

expand to see more

James is writing to people with wars and fightings among them, who ask and receive not because they ask amiss, and whom he calls adulterers for their friendship with the world. His prescription is Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness — followed immediately by Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up. The mourning is not an end but a road, and it leads to being lifted up. Against this, the ordinary evangelical service is engineered so that no one will ever be uncomfortable, and the pulpit’s first duty is understood to be warmth. The dictionary does not commend sourness; Psalm 126 is in the same canon and the laughter there is a mark of God’s work. It observes only that a ministry incapable of producing James 4:9 has removed a tool the apostles used.

Ecclesiastes 7:3 states the principle that makes sense of the whole: by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better. Sorrow does something for a man that mirth cannot, which is why the Preacher says it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting. This is not a preference for misery but an observation about what teaches. Proverbs 14:13 completes it from the other side, and anyone who has watched a room knows it is true: Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful. Laughter is often the sound a grief makes when it is not permitted to be heard, and a church that leaves no room for the house of mourning gives such people nowhere to go.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sechoq (H7814), laughter, derision; tsachaq (H6711), to laugh — the root of the name Isaac; Greek gelos (G1071), laughter; gelao (G1070), to laugh.

expand to see more

Hebrew sechoq (H7814) — laughter, and also derision; our mouth filled with laughter (Psalm 126:2).

Hebrew tsachaq (H6711) — to laugh; Sarah laughed, and the son was named Yitschaq, Isaac, he laughs (Genesis 21:6).

Hebrew holelah (H1947) — madness; I said of laughter, It is mad (Ecclesiastes 2:2).

Greek gelos (G1071) — laughter; only at James 4:9 in the New Testament.

Greek gelao (G1070) — to laugh; Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh (Luke 6:21).

Usage

"Then was our mouth filled with laughter (Psalm 126:2) — the involuntary praise of a delivered people."

"Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful (Proverbs 14:13) — the sound a grief makes when it may not be heard."

"Let your laughter be turned to mourning (James 4:9) — a call to repentance, and the road to being lifted up."
